title: Premise
body: Quoderat (from quod erat demonstrandum, "which was to be demonstrated") is a traditional fantasy world of wizards, magic and dragons where power determines status. It is a standalone project, separate from Jorange, set in a world that is not Earth; real history serves only as inspiration. Dungeons have been dropped because they don't fit.

title: Law Holders
body:
The top tier are gods who each embody one non-physical natural law, and every such law is unique: one holder at a time, set in stone.

- **Mathematical laws count**, such as a god of differentiation. Human-defined constants are not laws (for now), so Avogadro's number is out.
- **Differentiation and Integration** are mathematical inverses, so their gods have a built-in relationship.
- **What holding a law does:** a holder senses their law operating everywhere and can nudge how it manifests, but cannot rewrite it or stop others from using it. They also sense when someone is trying to disprove it, with the alarm scaling to how serious the attempt is, unless that person is hidden by a physical power that cloaks them completely. The cloak only hides people from law holders, and it belongs to the kitsune family, so any mortal can receive it as a totem.
- **Holding a law does not make you stronger in a fight.** A physical-power wielder can kill a law holder, and everyone can die. Some holders are ageless, but many things besides old age can kill.
- **Scope determines power, and power determines status.** There are countless minor gods with very unequal status. Status also has a second axis, impact factor: how much a law has shaped history and daily life. A narrow law with heavy impact can carry more prestige than its power alone suggests.
- **Laws can cause physical effects.** What holders can't wield is elemental power, which comes from the dragons, while laws are discovered through the app.
- **No elemental powers.** A holder can only wield them by permanently abandoning their law, which opens its test.
- **Day to day,** holders study their own law to find its flaws before anyone else does, and lesser holders plot power grabs against bigger ones.
- **Sublaws:** a law nested under another is separate but weaker. As a private author guideline, two laws are the same only if each overlaps the other by 80% or more, judged by what they govern rather than their form.
- **Disproof:** a holder claims a specific formulation of a law. Disproof has three outcomes. Partially disproven: the holder survives with a smaller law, and the disprover holds the disproven slice as a new law. Overridden (a broader law exposes a failure in this one): the holder dies, the old law's test opens, and the first disprover holds the new parent law above it (as relativity sits above Newton's gravity). Completely disproven: the test dies too, and the first disprover holds the law that replaces it. These apply even if several people disprove it at once, and the first disprover claims any new law, as with any first discovery. A holder who disproves or revises their own law inherits the result.
- **Demotion:** discovering a broader law that exposes no failure in an existing one simply makes the existing law its sublaw. The holder lives, demoted. One person can never hold two laws, but a holder can abandon their law to claim a higher one.
- **No disputes over held laws:** a law that already has a holder can't be discovered, so overlap disputes never arise in-world.
- **The Law of All Laws can be disproven,** but with no living holder, there is no one to kill. The first disprover gets the new law the disproof forms, which makes them a powerful holder with a stake in the system, not a contender for the app.
- **Sublaws under a disproven law** die with it only if they are disproven too. If the parent's scope merely shrinks, they survive and can expand into the domain it gave up.

title: Physical Powers and Dragons
body:
Physical (elemental) powers, inspired by Genshin's Visions, are open to everyone; only non-physical laws are unique.

- **The division is a metaphysical rule of the world,** defined as follows: laws are rules about how things behave, elemental powers are the things themselves, and sublaws sit entirely inside a bigger law. Grey zones like gravity sit in between, are decided case by case, and their category may shift over time.
- **Origin:** each family of physical power once belonged to one kind of mythical creature. Dragons held the elements, defined as the four states of matter (earth, water, air and plasma); others held families such as life and healing (unicorns), renewal (phoenixes), illusion and concealment (kitsune) and the body itself (trolls), with more to be added as needed. Law holders hunted all of them out of greed (for now, none escaped). The hunters hoped to take the power, but laws and physical powers are mutually exclusive. By the time they realized, the power had been released to every mortal. No mortal is born with physical power. Mortals receive it through totems that the world itself produces and gives to them (the slain creatures' power, soaked into the world and condensed back out), one totem per creature family, and a mortal can wield powers from more than one family.
- **Totems:** every mortal receives one at a certain age, chosen by the world as a fit for them, and more can arrive at random later. Totems can't be stolen or transferred. When the owner dies, the totem returns to the world.
- **Dragons today** are not extinct. Surviving creatures keep innate power that doesn't come from totems, which makes them stronger than mortals, but it is exclusive: they can't wield any other family's powers. They cannot grant or revoke powers. They resent the law holders, but they cannot hold laws themselves. They form an organized faction, with details to come.
- **Hybrids** (half-creatures, half-elves among them) are possible but rare: they are usually sterile, and creatures' hatred of mortals keeps unions scarce. A hybrid is born with innate power, the one exception to totems, and because it can never abandon its own blood, it can never hold a law. Hybrids can also receive totems. On a rough scale of depth, a totem gives 20–30, a full creature's innate power 90–100, and a hybrid's half-blood 40–60, which makes hybrids extremely powerful, rare and discriminated against. Where elves fit is still undecided.

title: The Test
body:
A law passes to whoever scores highest on its test, and every attempt is punished in proportion to how far the candidate got.

1. **Unclaimed laws:** discovery is the first test. Claiming is automatic: the discoverer holds the law and sets its test at the same moment.
2. **Each holder sets the next test** and a secret internal timer when they gain the law. Both stay secret while the holder is alive.
3. **The test must be about its law,** though a holder can build it around an obscure part of the law.
4. **The test opens on vacancy:** when the holder dies, permanently abandons the law, or is killed by its disproof. Anyone can attempt it, and the app announces it.
5. **Highest score wins, and the winner takes all.** The app does the scoring. Scores are hidden, but each candidate can sense their own progress. A candidate who dies has their score invalidated, so leaders must protect themselves. Everyone else's scores stay as they are.
6. **Punishment scales with progress,** even if the candidate quits partway, ranging from headaches to death. All punishments land at once, when there is a winner.
7. **The timer runs only while one candidate leads alone.** Any tie at the top, including zero-zero, pauses it. There is no sudden death: a tied law simply waits until someone pulls ahead.
8. **No attempts:** everyone is tied at zero, so the timer stays paused and the law waits indefinitely.
9. **Leaks are allowed:** a holder can secretly tell a chosen heir the test, so dynasties are possible.
10. **No reclaiming:** a holder who abandons a law gives it up permanently.

title: The App and the Law of All Laws
body:
The first law holder held the Law of All Laws. He discovered that mortals can wield laws to gain supernatural power and condensed that knowledge into the "app" (placeholder name): a cheap, mass-produced bracelet anyone can get. He released its instructions openly, so no one can monopolize it.

- **Everyone uses it.** The app announces when tests open and scores every attempt. People trust its scoring because everyone believes in it.
- **The app is his test.** To pass, a candidate must break the app open, which everyone believes means hacking in to control it or destroying the server it runs on.
- **No one has scored a single point** since his death. Every attempt scores zero, so it stays a zero-zero tie and the Law of All Laws remains vacant. A single point would start the timer and put that person in the lead alone.
- **Breaking the app is believed to stop everything,** which is why people don't go crazy for it. No one actually knows whether that's true, or what the winner would inherit.

title: Ordinary People and the Climb
body:
Ordinary people are on the same track as the gods, and the gods cannot stop every climber.

- **The path up** is finding a law, so scholars have a natural route to godhood.
- **There is always room at the top:** mathematics is effectively infinite, so unclaimed laws never run out.
- **Climbing costs something:** a mortal must give up physical power to hold a law.
- **Built-in tension:** dynastic heirs who were told the test compete against outsiders who attempt it blind.

title: Open Questions
body:
- [ ] Decide privately what the app test's winner inherits. In-world it stays a mystery.
- [ ] If the Law of All Laws is disproven: overridden keeps the app's test open beneath a new parent law; completely disproven kills the test. In-world scholars argue over which would happen.
- [ ] Where is the app's server, given anyone can build a bracelet from the open instructions?

title: How the Pantheon Is Ranked
body:
Scope determines power, and power determines status, so the most powerful people in the world are the holders of the broadest laws. The Law of All Laws is vacant, so the top tier begins just below it.

Laws are not limited to STEM. Social laws also count, but STEM laws come first here because they are easier to rank and objectively powerful.

title: Top-Tier Roster
body:
The top tier splits into three groups by how safe their laws are: logic as the quiet old guard, mathematics as the untouchable aristocracy, and physics as rich but nervous.

| Group | Law | Why it's powerful | Risk of disproof |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Logic | Non-Contradiction | Nothing can be both true and false; every other law depends on it | Nearly impossible |
| Logic | Excluded Middle | Every statement is true or false; just as broad | Contested: intuitionistic logic rejects it |
| Logic | Incompleteness | A law about the limits of laws (Gödel, 1931) | Proven, so very low |
| Mathematics | Number, Sets | The foundations all of mathematics is built on | Proven math can't be disproven |
| Physics | Conservation of Energy | Governs the entire physical world | Can be overridden |
| Physics | Entropy | Governs the entire physical world | Can be overridden |
| Physics | Causality | Governs the entire physical world | Can be overridden |

Holders for each are still to be defined.

title: The Law of Non-Contradiction
body:
The first law of the pantheon to be built out. It holds that nothing can be both true and false at the same time and in the same sense.

- **Scope:** every other law, in mathematics or physics, depends on it, which makes its holder arguably the most powerful living person in the world.
- **Safety:** it is nearly impossible to disprove, so the holder's main threat is physical rather than intellectual.

### The Holder

**Title: The Spear and Shield.** The Chinese word for contradiction, 矛盾 (máodùn), comes from the *Han Feizi*: a merchant claims his spear pierces anything and his shield blocks anything, and a bystander asks what happens when the spear hits the shield. He is the answer to that question.

- **Origin:** he discovered the law himself and has lived from that ancient time to the present through magic.
- **He has a cat.** Canon.

* **Longevity:** he refuses to let himself be both alive and dying, applying his own law to his body.
* **Era:** laws are discovered through the app, so he came after the first holder built it, which makes him one of the oldest people alive.
* **Nudging:** around him, uncertainty collapses. Doubt, bluffs and anything undecided are forced to resolve into a single answer.
* **Protection:** over his long life a dynasty has grown around him, and he hides inside it.
* **Day to day:** an old man with a cat. No one sees or hears of him 99.99% of the time, but he is always there.

title: The Law of the Excluded Middle
body:
Every statement is either true or false. Together with Non-Contradiction, it makes every statement exactly one of the two. It is as broad as Non-Contradiction but contested, since intuitionistic logic rejects it.

- **Holder:** Tertia, a young prodigy who inherited the law from her father. Her name comes from the law's Latin motto, tertium non datur, "no third option is given."
- **Lineage:** a long dynasty. Her father inherited from his great-grandmother, and so on back to a founder who was best friends with S&S (the Spear and Shield). Her ancestors died of many causes, not just old age.
- **Day to day:** unlike S&S, she is out in the world.
- **Natural threat:** the holder of Incompleteness. Gödel showed that some truths can never be proven, and to anyone who equates "true" with "provable," that leaves statements that are neither, which is exactly what this law denies.

* **Alliance:** her family has been allied with S&S since the founding friendship.
* **Nudging:** near her, the middle disappears. Fence-sitting, neutrality and "it's complicated" stop working, so everyone has to pick a side.

title: Incompleteness
body:
Any consistent system rich enough to do arithmetic contains truths it can't prove, and can't prove its own consistency (Gödel, 1931).

**Title: The Open Question.** S&S is where questions go to end; she is proof that some never will.

- **Origin:** self-made. She discovered the law herself only a few decades ago, a newcomer among ancients with no dynasty.
- **Nudging:** near her, no system can close. Every rulebook, contract, fortress plan or strategy develops a gap that no revision fully seals; things don't fail, but they are never airtight.
- **Protection:** no dynasty and no guards. Any plan made against her has a hole in it, so she survives by being impossible to fully plan around.
- **Day to day:** a flaw-finder for hire. Factions pay her to find loopholes in rivals' treaties and succession claims.
- **Flaw:** paranoia. Someone who sees the hole in every system eventually trusts none of them, including the people around her.
- **Ambition:** to partially disprove Excluded Middle and claim the slice she breaks off, perhaps a law of the undecidable. Tertia senses every attempt, so the two are locked in a duel of minds at a distance.
- **Relationships:** rival to Tertia, philosophical opposite of S&S. He forces answers, Tertia forces sides, and she guarantees there's always one question nobody can settle.

title: Number and Sets
body:
Number is ancient; Sets was discovered much later, and numbers turned out to be buildable from sets, which put Sets above Number.

### The Feud

1. **Sets is discovered.** Number becomes its sublaw overnight, demoting its first holder without killing him. The first holder of Sets then killed him by hand, and a new holder took Number.
2. **The paradox.** A descendant of that first Number holder finds a paradox inside the original Sets (in reality, Russell's paradox of 1901) and uses it to kill the first holder of Sets.
3. **The aftermath.**
   - **Number** is now held by the paradox-finder. He went into hiding and has not been found since. Rumor says he went to the dragons.
   - **Sets** sat empty for a long time until someone inherited it and elevated it with the fix (in reality, the stricter ZFC axioms). Full details to come.

### Sets: Ensa, the Restorer

Her name comes from the French *ensemble*, "set."

- **Origin:** Sets sat vacant for generations in a zero-zero tie. Ensa was the first to score and won, then revised her own law with the fix that makes the paradox impossible to state (in reality, Zermelo's 1908 axioms with later additions by Fraenkel and Skolem).
- **Nudging:** around her, belonging becomes definite: who is in a group, which faction someone serves, where a border falls. Her fixed law forbids a set of everything, so no group near her can claim to contain everything.
- **Signature legend:** her law includes the Axiom of Choice, whose strangest consequence (the Banach–Tarski paradox) lets a ball be cut and reassembled into two of the same size. Rumor says she once did it with a ball of gold.
- **Weak point:** the Axiom of Choice can be neither proven nor disproven from the other axioms (Cohen, 1963). That part of her law sits in the Open Question's territory.
- **Consequence for the feud:** restoring Sets put it back above Number, so the paradox-finder's law is a sublaw again and his revenge was quietly undone.
- **Day to day:** a builder rather than a fighter, sought out whenever a treaty, guild or kingdom needs a foundation. Close to the logic gods.

### Number: Ilar Hesabu, the Uncounted

His law operates everywhere, yet no one knows where he is. He still uses his family name, Hesabu (Swahili for arithmetic, counting), even under aliases, refusing to let hiding erase his ancestor a second time.

- **Origin:** raised in the murdered Number holder's diminished dynasty, among genealogies and account books, preparing for Number's test, which his family leaked to him. He is effectively ageless.
- **Nudging:** he pushes existing quantities toward exact allocations (grain settling into equal portions) while preserving totals. He can't create an extra portion or make a false equation true.
- **Protection:** he lives under a dragon's protection, revealed to very few. His law gives him information, not defense against a blade or poison.
- **Day to day:** repairs his host's accounts, teaches arithmetic, and insists every payment is correct, especially wages owed to servants. Patient with honest mistakes, suspicious of anyone who calls a discrepancy "negligible."
- **Flaw:** he mistook his family's grievance for a right to supremacy. Assuming Sets deserved no successor is the arrogance that made Ensa's restoration possible.
- **Ambition:** to win back Number's independence. He studies Ensa's foundations for a real failure, while fearing resentment is making him decide the answer in advance.
- **The dragons:** the rumor is true. Killing the first Sets holder earned him a hearing, not forgiveness, and his host makes him acknowledge the law holders' persecution of dragons as the price of sanctuary.

**The paradox.** The first holder of Sets was arrogant and sensed Ilar's attempt too late. The paradox exposed a failure, so it counted as an override: one stroke defeated one of the most powerful men of the age, and the next killed him. Sets' test opened, and any new law the paradox formed went unclaimed, since Ilar already held Number. Ever since, every holder has understood the importance of keeping their law clean.

**Relationships**

- **S&S:** respects him as the principle that made the paradox decisive, but avoids him, not wanting his own account of revenge put under the same scrutiny.
- **Tertia:** admires her speed, distrusts her readiness to turn every distinction into a confrontation.
- **The Open Question:** unsettled by her foothold in arithmetic, but sees her as an intellectual equal. She can't harm him: Incompleteness guarantees open questions inside arithmetic but never disproves it.
- **Ensa:** resents her most because she succeeded honestly, repairing the structure whose failure had vindicated him.

title: The Physics Trio
body:
Broad but overridable: physics holders are rich but nervous.

### Conservation of Energy: Voss Halloran, the Ledger-Keeper

Also called *The Closed Book* in older texts. Ageless in practice; he has looked sixty-five for well over a century.

- **Origin:** a miller's son who taught himself mathematics and discovered the law unclaimed, setting its test as he claimed it. He privately suspects he got there by reading rivals' work he shouldn't have seen.
- **Nudging:** an audit, not a command. He can't create, destroy or stop energy, but he can choose where a discrepancy goes: a fire's waste heat into the ground instead of the granary, as long as the total is unchanged. He can also sense where any loss went.
- **Protection:** he never fights. Contracts with three elemental mercenary companies, a quiet fortune, and a dozen holders who owe him favors for helping keep their laws clean. He doesn't live where he says he does.
- **Day to day:** honest ledgers in the morning, then long walks listening to the world add and subtract. A small house full of wound, inaccurate clocks. Dislikes being thanked.
- **Flaw:** he can't leave an account open, and he trusts tidy formulations over true ones.
- **Ambition:** to write a formulation so clean, and a test so hard, that his law stays closed for centuries after him. He refuses to name an heir.
- **Exposure:** high. A broader symmetry law above him would expose no failure, so it would only demote him, and he has quietly begun to prefer that. His favors and contracts would survive a demotion. On cosmic scales, though, his ledger doesn't obviously close, a pressure he can never leave alone. He could abandon his law to claim a higher one. The Law of Symmetry exists but is undiscovered: a vacant slot above every conservation law (energy, momentum, angular momentum). Its discovery would demote them all at once without killing anyone, and it is Voss's one way out, if he dares to abandon his law first.

### Entropy: Rudolf Ludwig, the Chancellor of Thermal Decay

- **Origin:** inherited through a meticulous dynastic bloodline going back to the law's discoverers.
- **Nudging:** probability bends under his focus, letting him speed up structural fatigue or briefly delay dispersal in a local system.
- **Protection:** industrial wealth funding paranoid sentinels who watch for anyone attempting Maxwell's-demon tricks against his law.
- **Day to day:** auditing engines, stamping out perpetual-motion schemes, and scrubbing his own formulation for the smallest paradox.
- **Flaw:** crushing anxiety rooted in the death of Sets' first holder, killed by a paradox he sensed too late.
- **Ambition:** to lock probability into certainty before a broader physics demotes him.
- **Exposure:** high. He claimed that entropy always increases, the strict formulation, and no one has disproven it yet. He is the god of endings, since entropy is the one process that can't be undone, and he is doomed to end badly: in reality, tiny systems briefly run backward, so the disproof that breaks him is out there waiting to be found.

### Causality: Rushd, the Uncertain Cause

- **Origin:** discovered. A philosopher-mathematician who formulated the law while wrestling with doubts about whether causation is real or only reliable correlation.
- **Nudging:** he can't reverse cause and effect, but he can choose which of the permitted effects a cause produces. Nothing he picks can break the speed of light.
- **Protection:** a small, loyal cadre of scholars and bodyguards, and constant revision of his own formulation to close gaps.
- **Day to day:** reviewing arguments about causation, mapping causal webs, refining his law's wording. He rarely intervenes in the world.
- **Flaw:** deep doubt about whether his law describes real necessity or mere correlation, which slows him to call a true counterexample a threat.
- **Ambition:** to revise causality into a purely logical truth that can't be disproven.
- **Exposure:** moderate to high. Quantum and relativistic edge cases offer endless apparent counterexamples that threaten but can't kill him; only a broader law of spacetime that exposes a real failure could, and a purely logical account of causation could demote him. Causality counts as a physics law, so it can be overridden.

title: Social Laws
body:
Smaller in scope than physics, since they only operate where people are, but they shape daily life directly. Most are tendencies with known exceptions, so their holders are the most exposed to partial disproof in the world. Where STEM gods are distant forces, social gods sit across the table from you. No rule bars a social law from climbing; in practice, scope keeps them below STEM.

### The Iron Law of Oligarchy: Aldous Vane, the Iron Clerk

Also called *Keeper of the Inevitable Few*. Every organization, however democratic at the start, ends up run by a small elite.

- **Origin:** inherited. His predecessor discovered the law watching his own commune centralize within a year, and set Vane's test: join a new trade guild and, without interfering, record the exact moment its assembly gave way to a permanent committee. Vane passed by predicting the committee's members three days early.
- **Nudging:** "letting the floor tilt." He thickens the friction of flat decision-making: longer agendas, harder-to-reach meeting halls, more technical minutes. Those with time drift to the center; everyone else drifts away.
- **Protection:** he never leads anything. He attaches to existing hierarchies as a clerk or secretary, and his heirs watch for flat experiments, joining them to disrupt from within or discrediting their records.
- **Day to day:** a records keeper in a port city's customs house, watching committees form and predicting who gets sidelined first. He keeps a ledger of flat organizations that collapsed into cliques.
- **Flaw:** bored by stability. He has sabotaged competent councils just to watch a new elite scramble into place, making enemies among holders who value predictability.
- **Ambition:** to join a truly flat organization that has lasted long enough to threaten him, and be present when the law reasserts itself.
- **Exposure:** high, through slow accumulation. His formulation says organizations "end up" ruled by a few, so temporary flatness only delays it; what chips at him is an organization that stays flat for its entire life. A large, long-lived one could demote him.

### Supply and Demand: Lian Xiu, the Equilibrium Sovereign

- **Origin:** inherited after her predecessor's death, with the law already wounded: the Giffen slice (goods whose demand rises with price) had been broken off and is held by someone else.
- **Nudging:** shifts supply chains and expectations to move market trends, but can't force outcomes.
- **Protection:** a network of economic analysts watching for anomalies; she avoids impoverished regions where Giffen behavior reappears.
- **Day to day:** travels between trade hubs, keeping markets balanced and watching for exceptions that could shrink her law.
- **Flaw:** overconfidence. She ignores early signs of new exceptions, like speculative bubbles or sudden demand surges.
- **Ambition:** to revise her own formulation so well that the Giffen holder's slice becomes redundant.
- **Exposure:** high. New market behaviors constantly threaten her, and the Giffen holder is a standing rival probing for weaknesses.

### Goodhart's Law: Mattias Krane, the Moving Target

When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

- **Origin:** discovered. A guild examiner who spent twenty years watching apprentices learn the exam instead of the craft, crystallized by a nail workshop that, paid by count, made thousands of useless tiny nails, and paid by weight, made a few enormous ones.
- **Nudging:** he senses every measure that has become a target. He can push one further from the truth (a quota's numbers rise while what it counts rots), or shield a measure by keeping people from noticing it judges them.
- **Protection:** he is unmeasurable. Any metric aimed at finding him (a bounty description, a ranking, a pattern of sightings) stops being reliable the moment it is used to hunt him.
- **Day to day:** hired by rulers to find which reports are lies, feared by guilds that hit their targets suspiciously well, and paid more by those who want to learn how to game a measure.
- **Flaw:** he can't want anything openly. The moment he sets a goal, he sees it becoming a target and starts gaming it himself.
- **The app's test:** he believes no one scores because everyone attempting it is targeting the score. To score a point, you would have to attempt the test without wanting to win, and he is the one person alive who can't stop wanting it.
- **Exposure:** high, through measures where gaming is improvement: a runner targeting a faster time simply gets faster. Anyone who formalizes that pattern could break off a slice of his law.

### To settle

- [ ] Settled: one person can't hold two laws. Killing Sets' holder let Number expand back into its lost status, so the paradox-finder left Sets alone, assuming it was finished, and it sat vacant.
- [ ] Settled: discovering a parent law only kills the holder beneath it if it exposes a failure in their law (as relativity did to Newton). Otherwise the old law is demoted to a sublaw and its holder lives.

title: How Creatures Work
body:
Each family of physical power once belonged to one kind of mythical creature. Law holders hunted all of them out of greed, hoping to take the power, but laws and physical powers are mutually exclusive, and the power was released into the world instead. The world now hands it out to mortals as totems: the slain creatures' power, soaked into the world and condensed back out.

- **Survivors keep innate power.** It doesn't come from totems and is far deeper than anything a mortal holds.
- **But it is exclusive.** A creature can't wield any other family's powers, and can never hold a law.
- **Depth scale (rough):** a single totem 20–30, a hybrid's half-blood 40–60, a full creature 90–100.
- **The balance:** creatures go deep (one family, very strong), mortals go wide (several weaker totems), and law holders go up (no physical power, only their law).

title: Dragons
body:
The former owners of the elements, each rooted in one state of matter but extending to its substance in any state (ice and steam stay water's, lava stays earth's), giving dragons a monopoly on all matter: earth (solids, from dirt to metals), water (liquids), air (gases, everything in the atmosphere) and plasma (fire and lightning).

- **Survived the hunt,** but lost their monopoly: the elements are now handed to mortals through totems, and every elemental totem is a fragment of their dead.
- **Innate elemental power** at full creature depth, but nothing beyond it.
- **They resent the law holders** and can never hold laws themselves.
- **An organized faction.**
- **Ilar Hesabu** (Number) lives under a dragon's protection. His host makes him acknowledge the law holders' persecution of dragons as the price of sanctuary.

### Society

- **An entire race,** numerous enough for a full society with multiple factions inside it.
- **Four tribes by element (earth, water, air, plasma), with ancient rivalries.** They have tried to set those aside for a united Dragons, without much success. Ideological factions cut across the tribes, drawing members from all of them.
- **Totem users are thieves** in dragon eyes, but most dragons accept they can do nothing about it and turn a blind eye. One faction hates this and would kill any totem user on sight.
- **Coexistence:** much time has passed, and most dragons are looking for a way to live peacefully with the rest of the world.
- **Ilar's hosts:** the earth tribe shelters him, believing a law holder gives them the upper hand in internal politics and a voice in the world outside.

title: Other Creature Families
body:
More families can be added as needed. Each pairing draws on real folklore.

| Creature | Family of power | Folklore root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unicorns | Life and healing | Medieval Europe believed unicorn horn neutralized poison |
| Phoenixes | Renewal | The self-renewing bird recorded by Herodotus |
| Kitsune | Illusion and concealment, including the cloak that hides people from law holders | Japanese fox spirits, masters of disguise |
| Trolls | The body itself: strength and endurance | Scandinavian trolls, enormously strong but turned to stone by sunlight |

title: Hybrids
body:
Half-creatures, half-elves among them. Possible but rare, much as a mortal holding several totem families is possible but rare.

- **Why rare:** hybrids are usually sterile (as a mule, the offspring of a horse and a donkey, almost always is), and creatures' hatred of mortals keeps unions scarce.
- **Innate power:** the one exception to totems. A hybrid is born with half-blood depth, 40–60 on the scale.
- **Totems too:** hybrids can also receive totems, stacking width on top of depth.
- **No laws, ever:** a hybrid can never abandon its own blood, so it can never hold a law.
- **Standing:** extremely powerful, rare and discriminated against from every side.
- **Elves:** where they fit is still undecided.

title: Ilar Hesabu
body:
His law operates everywhere, yet no one knows where he is. He still uses his family name, Hesabu (Swahili for arithmetic, counting), even under aliases, refusing to let hiding erase his ancestor a second time.

- **Origin:** raised in the murdered Number holder's diminished dynasty, among genealogies and account books, preparing for Number's test, which his family leaked to him. He is effectively ageless.
- **Nudging:** he pushes existing quantities toward exact allocations (grain settling into equal portions) while preserving totals. He can't create an extra portion or make a false equation true.
- **Protection:** he lives under a dragon's protection, revealed to very few. His law gives him information, not defense against a blade or poison.
- **Day to day:** repairs his host's accounts, teaches arithmetic, and insists every payment is correct, especially wages owed to servants. Patient with honest mistakes, suspicious of anyone who calls a discrepancy "negligible."
- **Flaw:** he mistook his family's grievance for a right to supremacy. Assuming Sets deserved no successor is the arrogance that made Ensa's restoration possible.
- **Ambition:** to win back Number's independence. He studies Ensa's foundations for a real failure, while fearing resentment is making him decide the answer in advance.
- **The dragons:** the rumor is true. Killing the first Sets holder earned him a hearing, not forgiveness, and his host makes him acknowledge the law holders' persecution of dragons as the price of sanctuary.

title: Ensa
body:
Her name comes from the French *ensemble*, "set."

- **Origin:** Sets sat vacant for generations in a zero-zero tie. Ensa was the first to score and won, then revised her own law with the fix that makes the paradox impossible to state (in reality, Zermelo's 1908 axioms with later additions by Fraenkel and Skolem).
- **Nudging:** around her, belonging becomes definite: who is in a group, which faction someone serves, where a border falls. Her fixed law forbids a set of everything, so no group near her can claim to contain everything.
- **Signature legend:** her law includes the Axiom of Choice, whose strangest consequence (the Banach–Tarski paradox) lets a ball be cut and reassembled into two of the same size. Rumor says she once did it with a ball of gold.
- **Weak point:** the Axiom of Choice can be neither proven nor disproven from the other axioms (Cohen, 1963). That part of her law sits in the Open Question's territory.
- **Consequence for the feud:** restoring Sets put it back above Number, so the paradox-finder's law is a sublaw again and his revenge was quietly undone.
- **Day to day:** a builder rather than a fighter, sought out whenever a treaty, guild or kingdom needs a foundation. Close to the logic gods.

title: Tertia
body:
Every statement is either true or false. Together with Non-Contradiction, it makes every statement exactly one of the two. It is as broad as Non-Contradiction but contested, since intuitionistic logic rejects it.

- **Holder:** Tertia, a young prodigy who inherited the law from her father. Her name comes from the law's Latin motto, tertium non datur, "no third option is given."
- **Lineage:** a long dynasty. Her father inherited from his great-grandmother, and so on back to a founder who was best friends with S&S (the Spear and Shield). Her ancestors died of many causes, not just old age.
- **Day to day:** unlike S&S, she is out in the world.
- **Natural threat:** the holder of Incompleteness. Gödel showed that some truths can never be proven, and to anyone who equates "true" with "provable," that leaves statements that are neither, which is exactly what this law denies.

* **Alliance:** her family has been allied with S&S since the founding friendship.
* **Nudging:** near her, the middle disappears. Fence-sitting, neutrality and "it's complicated" stop working, so everyone has to pick a side.
